question.prompt: Mrs. Jones is pouring orange juice into four identical glasses for her four sons. She fills the first three glasses completely but runs out of juice when the fourth glass is only \(\tfrac13\) full. What fraction of a glass must Mrs. Jones pour from each of the first three glasses into the fourth glass so that all four glasses will have the same amount of juice?

solutions.title: Find the equal share
solutions.explanation:
Moving juice between glasses preserves the total, so dividing that total by four gives the final amount in each glass.

Measure all amounts in units of one full glass. The total amount of juice is
\[
1+1+1+\frac13=\frac{10}{3}.
\]
Each glass must therefore contain
\[
\frac{10}{3}\div4=\frac{10}{3}\cdot\frac14=\frac56.
\]
Each initially full glass must contribute
\[
1-\frac56=\boxed{\frac16}
\]
of a glass, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Match the final amounts
solutions.explanation:
Each full glass loses one contribution, while the fourth glass receives three contributions. Comparing their final amounts gives an equation.

Let \(x\) be the fraction of a full glass poured from each of the first three glasses. Each of those glasses ends with \(1-x\), and the fourth ends with \(\frac13+3x\). Equal amounts require
\[
1-x=\frac13+3x.
\]
Adding \(x\) and subtracting \(\frac13\) on both sides gives
\[
\frac23=4x,
\qquad
x=\frac23\div4=\frac16.
\]
Thus Mrs. Jones must pour \(\boxed{\frac16}\) of a glass from each full glass, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
